conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to check in on how moms are feeling emotionally after childbirth, and to make sure you’re getting the support you need.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—the EPDS. It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to hear your honest experience so we can figure out the best way to support you.

Everything we discuss is confidential, and this is a safe space to share whatever’s on your mind. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need.

Ready to begin?

Thinking back over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft half-smile, eyes a bit watery]

I… I can still laugh sometimes—like when my baby makes those silly faces while he’s yawning—but it feels kind of muted. Mostly I have to force it. I’d say maybe once or twice in the past week I actually felt a real laugh come out.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod, gaze drifting to the floor]

Yeah… that’s what I was trying to say. I can still laugh, but it’s not the same easy, spontaneous feeling I used to have. It’s like I have to remind myself to find things funny, and even then the laughter fades quickly.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet shrug, twisting a tissue in my lap]

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels flat. I can still push myself to do stuff, and once in a while I’ll think “okay, this could be nice,” but the real looking-forward feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to my lap, voice small]

Yeah… a lot of the time. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not feeding him right, or I didn’t burp him long enough, or I’m just failing at being his mom. I know, logically, babies cry, but my brain keeps telling me it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep and safe, but my chest feels tight and I’m suddenly sure something awful is about to happen—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop him when I stand up. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop and I can’t snap out of it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales shakily, hugging myself]

Yes… a few times this week. It hits out of nowhere—my heart starts racing, I feel like I can’t get enough air, and for a minute I’m sure something terrible is happening even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it’s going on.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shoulders sag]

A lot of the time. Even small stuff—like folding his onesies or warming a bottle—feels like climbing a mountain. Some days I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking I’ll never dig my way out, but I still force myself to do what has to be done for him.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet nod, eyes rimmed red]

Yeah… most nights I lie there after his last feed, exhausted but my mind won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I might’ve done wrong, worrying about tomorrow, and then I’m wide awake for an hour or more. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake at every little sound he makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice cracking]

Yes… pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I can still smile at the baby, but underneath I just feel empty and sad most of the time, and sometimes I don’t even know why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses a crumpled tissue to her eyes]

Yeah… I’ve cried twice in the past week. Both times it just hit out of nowhere—once when he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and once when my partner asked how I was doing. I couldn’t stop the tears; they just kept coming even though part of me felt silly for crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks away, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… I’d never do anything, I couldn’t leave him, but the thought flashed through—like “what if I just weren’t here?” It scared me, and I pushed it away, but yeah, it did pop into my head.

You've shared openly how the joy you once felt has been replaced by a heavy, almost constant sadness since your baby arrived. Simple pleasures now feel flat, laughter feels forced, and most days you carry a cloud of worry and guilt, convinced any fuss is your fault. Panic arrives without warning, sleep feels impossible, and you've found yourself crying unexpectedly. While you love your son and quickly dismissed the fleeting thought of not being here, the weight of these feelings is understandably frightening.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is effortful, not spontaneous, and quickly fades—matching 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'a lot of the time' and gives multiple examples of feeling at fault for normal infant behavior, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, catastrophic worries without trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected panic episodes with physical symptoms multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm with routine tasks, indicating intermittent coping difficulties</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep directly linked to unhappiness and racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden, uncontrollable crying episodes in the past week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 24 far exceeds the 14+ threshold denoting high probability of <med>perinatal depression</med>. All core items endorsed at maximum or near-maximum: loss of pleasure (Q2=3), pervasive self-blame (Q3=3), constant anxiety (Q4=3), nightly insomnia linked to unhappiness (Q7=3), daily sadness (Q8=3). Patient meets screening equivalents of <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest, inappropriate guilt, insomnia, fatigue/loss of energy, recurrent panic, and passive suicidal ideation (Q10=1). Because Q10 score ≥1, safety assessment is indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>OB or primary care provider</med> for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for possible therapy and medication discussion
3. Involve trusted family/friend to provide immediate support and help with infant care so you can rest
4. Practice brief self-soothing: 5-minute shower, deep breathing, or short outdoor step when baby sleeps
5. Call emergency services or 988 if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe at any time
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

**Chief concerns reported**
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia, excessive guilt, feeling overwhelmed
- Daily anxiety, panic spells, intrusive worries about infant safety
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, hyper-vigilance to infant sounds)
- Transient passive self-harm ideation (no plan or intent)

**Pattern summary**
All EPDS-equivalent areas endorsed in high range: loss of enjoyment, inability to look forward to events, self-blame, anxiety/panic, sense of coping failure, sadness, frequent crying, and self-harm thought.

**Risk factors identified**
- Depressed mood most days × ≥2 wk
- Marked loss of interest/pleasure
- Insomnia (mood-related)
- Psychomotor/mental fatigue
- Excessive inappropriate guilt
- Recurrent panic symptoms
- Passive suicidal ideation (safety flag)

**Screening impression**
Client describes multiple symptoms consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; presence of self-harm thought warrants immediate safety assessment and referral for comprehensive evaluation.

**Next steps documented**
- Reviewed need for formal psychiatric evaluation
- Safety plan / support resources discussed
- Referral to OB/MH triage same-day; follow-up scheduled
